ME-WE.focus: Free-ranging wildlife, populations, habitats and professional field methods.
ME-WE.experience: Required Field Ecology and Scientific Communication, vertebrate biology lab, and a May-term Wildlife Field Survey provide a defined fieldwork sequence.
study: Wildlife Population Dynamics and Conservation with lab (required)
consider: Habitat, plant identification, statistics and policy occupy substantial curriculum space.
For zoo husbandry or training goals, plan a separate managed-animal placement.

ME-ZOO.focus: Broad animal biology, from cells and physiology to diversity and ecology.
ME-ZOO.experience: Hands-on laboratory and field courses are part of the degree. Faculty laboratory or field research can also be taken for credit or pursued through paid opportunities.
consider: Upper-level electives shape the specialty; Ecology is an optional concentration.
Compare available research projects with the sustained husbandry experience needed for animal-care goals.

UMA-BIO.focus: A flexible biology foundation that can be shaped toward behavior and organismal science.
UMA-BIO.experience: The elective requirements include two laboratory or field courses. The ecology course guide includes Animal Behavior with lab, organismal labs and field biology; research and placements add further experience.
consider: Ecology and behavior are elective directions, not an official named track.
Choose animal-focused courses and faculty projects deliberately; the major also includes plant and molecular biology.

UMA-WEC.focus: Wildlife conservation combining animal populations, habitat management and spatial analysis.
UMA-WEC.experience: Hands-on field skills are part of the concentration. The curriculum includes Wildlife Sampling and Identification, habitat management and GIS; summer jobs and internships extend the field experience.
consider: This is a concentration within Natural Resources Conservation.
Plan upper-level choices against Wildlife Society certification coursework; habitat, plants and policy are substantial components.

UMA-VT.focus: Veterinary nursing and technical care, including clinical and research-animal settings.
UMA-VT.experience: Laboratory and animal-science work in Amherst leads into advanced clinical coursework, community clinic practica and senior internships in the Newton portion of the program.
study: Anesthesia, surgery support and diagnostic imaging
consider: Students spend two years in Amherst, then two at the Charles River Campus in Newton.
The curriculum covers companion, large and laboratory animals; zoo/exotic experience needs targeted electives or placements.

UNE-AB.focus: Animal behavior through biology, psychology, learning and cognition.
UNE-AB.experience: A required Animal Behavior Internship/Research course and Animal Learning and Behavior lab provide structured experience. Placement examples include wildlife centers, service-dog organizations and aquariums.
study: Animal Learning and Behavior with lab (required)
consider: Compare the day-to-day duties of an internship with the methods used in a faculty research project.
For field-wildlife goals, plan additional GIS, habitat and population-methods coursework.

URI-AZ.focus: Managed-animal science with a zoo/aquarium certificate adding behavior, training and welfare.
URI-AZ.experience: The certificate requires Zoo Animal Management at Roger Williams Park Zoo and an internship-linked practicum. Practicum enrollment requires a concurrent or recently completed zoo/aquarium internship.
study: Advanced Methods in Applied Animal Behavior (certificate requirement)
Zoo and Aquarium Animal Welfare (certificate requirement)
consider: The Animal Science option retains domestic and livestock content.
Plan certificate prerequisites and the internship; the zoo-based course has additional costs.

URI-W.focus: Wildlife biology and conservation centered on free-ranging animals and their habitats.
URI-W.experience: Wildlife Field Techniques is required. Research, internships and other experiential courses can contribute toward concentration and supporting-elective requirements.
study: Mammalogy, Herpetology or Animal Behavior (concentration choices)
consider: Botany, habitat and natural-resource coursework are part of the route.
For managed-animal care, compare this major with the version that adds the zoo/aquarium certificate.

URI-WZ.focus: Wildlife field science paired with zoo/aquarium management, behavior and welfare.
URI-WZ.experience: The wildlife major includes required field techniques. The certificate adds zoo-based management coursework and a practicum tied to a concurrent or recently completed zoo/aquarium internship.
study: Zoo and Aquarium Animal Welfare (certificate requirement)
consider: Map certificate prerequisites, internship timing and course overlap with an advisor.
The wildlife core still includes plants, habitats and conservation; the zoo-based course adds costs.

CAN-ABEC.focus: Behavior and conservation with a Zoo Biology minor for captive-animal management.
CAN-ABEC.experience: Credit-bearing animal internships are available. The Zoo Biology minor offers zoo/aquarium internships, husbandry and enrichment among its elective choices; the minor alone does not require every one of them.
study: Zoo Animal Husbandry or Animal Enrichment (minor electives)
consider: The minor is 18 credits: one required management course plus 15 elective credits.
Choose husbandry, welfare and internship electives deliberately and plan their course rotation.

UNH-ZOO.focus: Broad zoology with room to specialize in physiology, behavior, ecology or aquatic systems.
UNH-ZOO.experience: A senior capstone is required: an approved experience plus BIOL 780. The experience can be a thesis, mentored research, internship or designated capstone course.
study: Field or laboratory research; senior capstone
consider: Choose the capstone route to match the kind of animal work wanted.
Husbandry, zoo management and clinical nursing are not the organizing core; add relevant placements for those goals.

DELVAL-ZOO.focus: Zoo science spanning husbandry, behavior, training, health and facility management.
DELVAL-ZOO.experience: Animal work begins in the first year. The Experience360 program includes internships in animal care and public education.
consider: A focused zoo-science curriculum leaves less generality than broad biology or zoology.
Compare the species and responsibilities available through animal-care internships.

UMA-BGR-VT.focus: Veterinary technical skills and patient care through associate or bachelor study in Bangor.
UMA-BGR-VT.experience: Onsite teaching facilities support hands-on technical skills and laboratory practice. The curriculum prepares students for clinical animal-care work.
study: Clinical patient care and animal handling
consider: Compare the associate and bachelor sequences and their credentialing milestones.
The program serves veterinary care broadly; seek specific placements for zoo or wildlife interests.

CANTON-VT.focus: Veterinary technology with companion, farm and laboratory animals.
CANTON-VT.experience: The B.S. includes the veterinary-technology associate curriculum, hands-on animal work and two clinical preceptorships. The first mandatory preceptorship is 120 hours.
study: Research Animal Techniques and clinical pathology
consider: Evaluate comfort with farm and laboratory animals as well as companion species.
Advanced bachelor coursework builds on the associate core; zoo medicine is a possible setting rather than a dedicated specialization.

DELHI-VT.focus: An associate-to-bachelor veterinary-technology route with live-animal clinical training.
DELHI-VT.experience: Live-animal labs begin in the first semester of the associate program. Teaching facilities include clinical and surgical suites, diagnostic imaging, laboratory-animal facilities and a large-animal farm.
study: Advanced clinical, laboratory-animal or public-health electives in the B.S.
consider: Entry to the B.S. follows an accredited veterinary-technology associate degree and separate admission requirements.
The animal mix is broader than zoo/exotics; compare placement options for that specialty.
